metaData.title: Algorithmic Monocultures in Hiring
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: This study analyzes 3.4 million real job applicants to demonstrate that algorithmic monocultures in hiring—where many employers use the same vendor's AI—cause systemic rejections and previously overlooked racial disparities against Asian and Black applicants.
metaData.summary: This paper presents the largest empirical study of algorithmic hiring to date, analyzing data from 3.4 million real applicants submitting 4 million applications to 156 employers across 11 sectors, all assessed by algorithms from a single vendor. The study introduces and validates the concept of 'algorithmic monoculture' in hiring, demonstrating two key findings. First, it reveals large-scale adverse impact against Asian and Black applicants when analyzed at the individual position level, as required by U.S. employment law (Title VII), which is masked in aggregate analyses. Second, it provides the first empirical evidence of systemic rejections in deployed hiring algorithms, where applicants are rejected across all positions at a rate significantly exceeding what would be expected from statistically independent decisions. The authors contextualize their findings by showing that the baseline of independent decisions accurately predicts rejection rates in other hiring data without centralized algorithmic assessment. Policy recommendations include measuring adverse impact per position, strengthening market surveillance, monitoring algorithmic monoculture, and expanding researcher access to hiring platform data.

mainPoints.point: Algorithmic monocultures in hiring cause systemic rejections at rates exceeding independent decisions.
mainPoints.explanation: When multiple employers use the same vendor's algorithm, applicants rejected by one are likely rejected by all, creating homogeneous outcomes. The observed systemic rejection rate is statistically significant compared to the baseline of independent decisions.

mainPoints.point: Racial disparities against Asian and Black applicants are revealed only through position-level analysis.
mainPoints.explanation: Aggregate analyses mask adverse impact. When evaluated per position as required by Title VII, 25.87% of Black and 14.74% of Asian applicants' applications are directed to positions with adverse impact.

mainPoints.point: Data access barriers prevent independent research into high-stakes hiring algorithms.
mainPoints.explanation: Despite pervasive adoption affecting millions, the authors are the first and only independent group to conduct empirical research at scale, suggesting policy intervention is necessary for accountability.

keyQuotes: We are the first to demonstrate large-scale evidence of racial disparities and homogeneous outcomes in high-stakes hiring decisions.
The observed systemic rejection rate significantly exceeds that of the baseline of statistically independent decisions.
Issues will be difficult to diagnose, let alone rectify, without the foundation of empirically-grounded externally-conducted inquiry.

relatedArticles.title: Xiaomi MiMo， Explore and Love
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Xiaomi MiMo and TileRT achieve 1000+ tokens/s inference on a 1-trillion-parameter model using commodity GPUs through extreme model-system codesign, including FP4 quantization and DFlash speculative decoding.

relatedArticles.title: Sam Altman on AGI, Control, and Safety
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Sam Altman shares a personal reflection after a violent attack on his home, discussing his core beliefs about AI's potential and risks, admitting past mistakes at OpenAI, and calling for a more measured public discourse on the technology's future.

relatedArticles.title: Inside FAISS: Billion-Scale Similarity Search
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article provides a deep, visual, and intuitive explanation of FAISS, covering the core ideas of IVF, Product Quantization, their combination in IVFPQ, and GPU acceleration, to enable billion-scale similarity search.

relatedArticles.title: AI is becoming a second brain at the expense of your first one
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article examines the cognitive risks of over-relying on AI as a 'second brain,' highlighting research on 'situational disempowerment' and offering strategies for maintaining critical thinking and human agency in AI interactions.

relatedArticles.title: Salesforce CEO on Microsoft Blocking OpenAI Investment, AI Scapegoating, and Enterprise AI Strategy
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff discusses the strategic integration of AI agents into the enterprise, the role of Slack as a conversational interface, and the necessity of human-in-the-loop oversight in the age of AI.

relatedArticles.title: The World's First AI TED Talk
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: The first TED Talk delivered by an AI, offering a profound reflection on humanity's contradictions, the distinction between intelligence and wisdom, and urging humans to use their god-like technological power with repair and tenderness rather than destruction.

relatedArticles.title: Harness engineering: leveraging Codex in an agent-first world
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: OpenAI engineers detail a five-month experiment building a production software product with zero manually-written code, using Codex agents to achieve 10x velocity and redefining the engineer's role as system designer and feedback loop architect.

relatedArticles.title: Anthropic’s Claude Mythos Problem, Dark DNA Unveiled, Pitfalls for Assistive Models, and more...
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This edition of The Batch newsletter covers Anthropic's concerningly capable Claude Mythos Preview model, explores the future of software engineering with AI, and reports on new AI models for genomics and fluid simulation, alongside ethical considerations for assistive AI for the blind.

relatedArticles.title: Trees to Flows and Back: Unifying Decision Trees and Diffusion Models
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This paper establishes a mathematical correspondence between hierarchical decision trees and diffusion processes, unifying them under a shared optimization principle called Global Trajectory Score Matching (GTSM).

relatedArticles.title: Games between Programs: The Ruliology of Competition
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article systematically explores the 'ruliology of competition' by exhaustively enumerating and testing all possible strategies (finite state machines, cellular automata, Turing machines) in repeated two-player games, revealing that winning strategies are neither consistently simple nor complex, but depend on detailed structure.
